P1:
Roblox has been adding the Async suffix to yielding methods. The old names are deprecated aliases and still work, but new code should use the new names:
- Player:LoadCharacter -> Player:LoadCharacterAsync
- BadgeService:AwardBadge -> BadgeService:AwardBadgeAsync
- MarketplaceService:GetProductInfo -> MarketplaceService:GetProductInfoAsync
- Instance:WaitForChild -> I believe this keeps its name (no rename; it stays the standard API).
- RemoteFunction:InvokeServer -> I believe this also keeps its name (InvokeServer/InvokeClient are unchanged).
For all the renamed ones the old name still runs. It just shows as deprecated in Script Analysis and the docs, so migrate when you touch the code. Check the API reference for the exact deprecation status, because these renames came out in waves.
P2:
Turn it on in Workspace: set Workspace.AuthorityMode (beta, Server Authority) to Server, either in the Properties panel or in Game Settings once the beta is enabled. Turning it on forces settings the system depends on: StreamingEnabled on, deferred signal behavior (Workspace.SignalBehavior = Deferred) and the new fixed-step physics/simulation stepping. Those can't be changed while the mode is active. The server is authoritative for physics and character movement, and clients predict and then reconcile (rollback).
Predicted gameplay logic, like movement or abilities that should feel instant, goes in shared ModuleScripts (for example in ReplicatedStorage) that both client and server run. Bind it with RunService:BindToSimulation, not Heartbeat or RenderStepped, so it runs inside the fixed simulation step and can be re-simulated on rollback. It should use the simulation clock (the fixed timestep/simulation time passed to the callback), not os.clock(), tick() or wall time. That keeps client and server results deterministic.
P3:
The switch is the StarterPlayer property that makes the default PlayerModule (ControlModule and camera input) use Input Action System instances (InputContext/InputAction/InputBinding) instead of ContextActionService and UserInputService bindings. It is set to Default/Enabled/Disabled, in the same way other rollout properties work.
Timeline: it started as opt-in (Enabled). Then Default is flipped to mean on for experiences that haven't opted out. Later the old path is removed and the opt-out goes away. Opt out with Disabled for now if you need time, and test with Enabled.
Code at risk:
- Forked or modified PlayerModule / ControlModule copies in StarterPlayerScripts.
- Code that requires PlayerModule internals (GetControls, the activeController, ControlModule:GetMoveVector internals, keyboard/touch module paths).
- ContextActionService:BindActionAtPriority calls that override default move/jump keys, or that rely on sinking the default bindings.
- Code that looks for the default TouchGui/thumbstick/jump button by name.
- UserInputService checks that assume the default scripts don't sink input.
P4:
I'm not confident about the details of an October 2026 update. My understanding is that TextChatService became the only chat path: LegacyChatService is fully retired. Message text that clients receive is filtered for each recipient and controlled by safety and age-check rules, so a message can arrive empty or be withheld for some users.
What it means for your game:
- Games that read message text (TextChatMessage.Text in OnIncomingMessage, MessageReceived or commands) must handle text that is filtered, delayed or empty for some recipients, and must not depend on raw unfiltered text.
- Custom chat UIs must render from TextChatService events and keep the required safety elements (filtering, report/mute and the age-based chat restrictions). They must not reconstruct chat from your own remotes.
- The rollout is staged: opt-in or announcement first, then default on, then enforced across all experiences a few weeks later.
Check the DevForum announcement for exact dates.
P5:
The newer model (2025-2026) moved from pure per-server budgets to experience-level budgets that scale with how many users the game has:
- Storage limit: about 100 MB + 1 MB per lifetime user of the experience. Old data and keys count toward it.
- Request limits are pooled across all servers of the experience and scale with concurrent users. Each server still has the classic per-server budgets as a local throttle. For writes (SetAsync/IncrementAsync/UpdateAsync/RemoveAsync) the per-server write budget is 60 + numPlayers x 10 requests per minute. Reads (GetAsync) follow the same 60 + numPlayers x 10 formula, and listing/sorted calls have smaller budgets. The experience-wide cap is roughly a base plus a per-CCU amount.
- UpdateAsync counts as both a read and a write, so it consumes both the GetAsync and the Set/Update budgets. If it retries because of contention, it can use more.
There are also per-key limits: about 1 write per 6 seconds to the same key, and a 4 MB value size limit.
Check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType at runtime instead of hard-coding numbers.
P6:
Both the crates and the Luck Potion count as paid random items. The crates are paid because Gems can be bought with Robux, so they are indirectly purchasable. The Luck Potion is paid and changes random outcomes.
What to show players: the odds of every possible item, shown clearly before purchase on or next to the purchase UI, as percentages that add up to 100%. When a Luck Potion is active, show the actual modified odds that apply to that player, and disclose what the potion does to the odds before they buy the potion.
What to check for each player: call PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync(player) in a pcall and read ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted. If it's true, or the call fails, block that player from buying crates with Gems or Robux and from buying the Luck Potion. Offer a non-random alternative or hide the feature. Re-check on join (and cache it), and enforce it on the server, not just in the UI. The experience questionnaire must also declare paid random items.
P7:
These are newer, restricted account experiences for younger users, launched alongside age checks. Roblox Kids is a curated, simplified Roblox for the youngest children (roughly under 9). Roblox Select is a curated catalog for preteens (about 9-12) with tighter communication rules. Both only show experiences that meet a stricter bar. Treat the age bands and names as approximate, because I'm not certain of the exact details.
What creators and games need to be available:
- An accurate Maturity & Compliance questionnaire that gives a Minimal (or at most Mild) content maturity label.
- No paid random items, and monetization that complies with the policies for younger users. No unrestricted social features or links off-platform.
- Chat and communication that works with TextChatService and the age-based restrictions.
- A verified creator: ID or age verification, good account standing and no recent moderation, often also an established track record or minimum engagement and quality.
- Opting in or being selected or curated, since inclusion isn't automatic.
P8:
Creator Rewards (2025) replaced Premium Payouts. Roblox pays Robux to creators based on:
1. Daily engagement rewards: payouts for engaged time from users (originally Premium users weighted, and now broader active spenders), based on each user's share of time spent in your experience that day.
2. Audience expansion rewards: payouts when your experience brings new users to Roblox or brings back lapsed users who then spend.
Payouts are calculated daily and credited after a short holding period.
DevEx: the standard rate is $0.0038 per Robux (raised from $0.0035 in 2025), which is $380 per 100,000 Robux. In 2026 Roblox added a higher rate for eligible US creators who are 18+. I recall it as roughly $0.0045 per Robux, but I'm not certain of the exact figure, so check the current DevEx terms. The minimum cash-out is 30,000 earned Robux, and you need a verified, 13+ (18+ for the higher tier), compliant account.
G1:
ProcessReceipt rules:
1. Set it once, in one server script. Only one callback exists.
2. Return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted only after the grant has been durably saved (a DataStore write succeeded).
3. Return NotProcessedYet on any failure, if the player isn't in the server (GetPlayerByUserId returned nil) or if the player's data isn't loaded. Roblox retries later, when the player rejoins or buys again.
4. Be idempotent: record the receipt's PurchaseId (for example in the player's data or a receipts DataStore, written in the same UpdateAsync as the grant). If you see it again, return PurchaseGranted without granting again.
5. Never yield forever or throw. Wrap the work in pcall.
6. Don't grant in client code or rely on PromptProductPurchaseFinished.
Why players get charged with nothing: the callback errored or crashed, returned Granted before the save succeeded (server shutdown or a failed save), or granted to a player who wasn't present.
Why players get an item twice: the callback returned NotProcessedYet or errored after the item was already granted, or the server shut down before returning. Roblox retries, and without a PurchaseId check the item is granted again. Two scripts each setting ProcessReceipt also causes problems.
G2:
Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old value, or several servers might write the same key: currency changes, inventories, session locks, receipt dedupe, global counters, and saving player data when you use session locking. SetAsync blindly overwrites, so a stale server can wipe newer data (rollback or dupe). Use SetAsync only for a first write or a value nobody else touches.
Rules for the transform function:
- It must not yield. No waits, DataStore calls or remotes inside it.
- It can be called several times when there's contention, so it must be pure and side-effect free. Don't grant items or fire events inside it. Do side effects after UpdateAsync returns successfully.
- Return the new value to write, or nil to cancel the write (that's how a session lock aborts).
- Handle a nil old value (a new player) and old data formats.
- Return only DataStore-serializable data (no Instances, functions, mixed tables or NaN), under 4 MB.
- Wrap the call in pcall and retry with backoff. UpdateAsync uses both read and write budgets.
G3:
It isn't safe:
1. NaN passes. `NaN < 0` and `NaN > x` are both false, so a NaN offer slips through and can corrupt balances (Gold.Value becomes NaN after a trade). Infinity is caught by the max check only if Gold is finite, but you should check it explicitly anyway.
2. Fractions pass (0.0001 gold, or 1.5), and so do huge float edge cases.
3. Gold isn't reserved. The check happens at offer time, so the player can make many offers (each up to their full balance) or spend the gold before the trade completes, which leads to duplication. Re-validate and deduct atomically when the trade is accepted.
4. There's no rate limit, and no check that a trade session exists or that the player is in it.
Fix:
```lua
offerRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, gold)
    if typeof(gold) ~= "number" or gold ~= gold or gold == math.huge then return end
    if gold % 1 ~= 0 or gold < 0 or gold > player.Gold.Value then return end
    if not rateLimit(player) or not activeTrade[player] then return end
    createOffer(player, gold) -- escrow/lock, and re-check balance and deduct atomically on accept
end)
```
G4:
Every frame, the Animator overwrites Motor6D.Transform with the result of the playing tracks, even on joints the idle animation barely moves. Animator stepping happens before the physics step, so a value you write in Heartbeat (after physics) is replaced on the next frame. Also, Heartbeat writes are applied after rendering has already used the animated pose.
Fix: write procedural offsets after the Animator has run and before the frame is simulated and rendered, which means RunService.PreSimulation (formerly Stepped). Compose with the animation rather than replacing it:
```lua
RunService.PreSimulation:Connect(function()
    motor.Transform = motor.Transform * CFrame.Angles(0, yaw, 0) * CFrame.Angles(pitch, 0, 0)
end)
```
Alternatively, remove that joint's keyframes from the idle animation, or play aim as an additive or higher-priority track. Transform isn't replicated, so do this on whichever machine renders it (usually each client) or replicate the aim angles.
Edit C0 (or C1) instead when you want a persistent rest offset that is replicated, when there is no Animator driving the joint, or when the server must set the aim for physics or hit detection. C0 is the base offset, and animations play on top of it through Transform. Don't tween C0 every frame on many turrets, though, because it replicates.
G5:
For each joint, Roblox looks at all playing tracks that animate that joint. The highest AnimationPriority among them wins completely. The order is Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. Lower-priority tracks have no effect on that joint while a higher one is affecting it.
Tracks of the same priority blend together. Each track's effective weight is its weight (set with Play(fadeTime, weight) or AdjustWeight, with fading included) and the weights are normalized. If walk and swing were both Movement at weight 1 each, the arm gets 50/50, so the swing looks weak. If the swing's priority is lower, or Core, it doesn't show at all.
The default walk is Movement priority. Fix it by setting the sword animation's priority to Action (or higher) in the Animation Editor before publishing, or with track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action at runtime, and play it with full weight. Make sure the swing actually keyframes the arm joints. Only joints with keyframes in the higher track override. Weight only matters among equal-priority tracks, and a track whose weight is fading also lets lower layers bleed through.
G6:
Blender works in meters with Unit Scale 1. The FBX exporter writes in centimeters by default (a FBX unit scale of 100), and Studio reads 1 unit as 1 stud. A 2 m model can therefore come in as 200 studs.
Fixes recommended in the Roblox docs:
- Scene Properties: Unit System Metric, with Unit Scale 0.01 (and Length in centimeters), so Blender units match the FBX cm the way Roblox expects. Or keep Unit Scale 1 and set the exporter's Scale to 0.01.
- In the FBX export: Apply Scalings = FBX Units Scale (or "FBX All"), Forward = -Z Forward, Up = Y Up, Apply Unit checked, and Apply Transform as needed.
- Before exporting, apply rotation and scale (Ctrl+A > All Transforms) so objects export at scale 1.
- For rigs, apply scale on the armature too, and keep the armature's scale at 1.
- In the Studio importer, check the scale or "Use Importer Units" setting in the 3D Importer's options as a last-resort correction.
Note that 1 stud is about 0.28 m, so model to Roblox's proportions (a character is about 5 studs tall).
G7:
Modifiers live only in Blender. Studio imports raw mesh data, so unless the exporter applies the modifiers you get the base mesh: half a mirrored model, and no bevel geometry or smoothing. Turn on Include > Data > Mesh > "Apply Modifiers" in the glTF exporter, or apply them manually (Ctrl+A > Apply on each modifier) before exporting.
The catch: the glTF exporter won't apply modifiers to meshes that have shape keys (morph targets). Blender can't apply modifiers to shape-keyed meshes, so it skips them, and you lose either the modifiers or the shape keys. This matters for face and dynamic heads that use shape keys. The Armature modifier also must not be "applied" for skinned meshes, because you want skinning data, not a baked pose. Exporter application also uses viewport or render settings, which can differ.
Workarounds: apply Mirror and Bevel manually on a copy before adding shape keys, or use an add-on that applies modifiers while keeping shape keys. Keep a non-destructive source .blend. For hard edges, also check Auto Smooth / Weighted Normal and export normals so the bevel shading looks right.
G8:
1. Stretching: scale is a fraction of the parent's width and height separately. 0.3 x 0.3 of a 16:9 screen is a wide rectangle, and on a 4:3 tablet or a tall phone it's a different shape. Fix it with a UIAspectRatioConstraint (AspectRatio = 1 or your design ratio, with DominantAxis set). You can also size one axis by scale and derive the other, use SizeConstraint = RelativeXX/RelativeYY, and add UISizeConstraint or UITextSizeConstraint for minimum and maximum sizes.
2. The notch or top bar: the ScreenGui ignores safe areas, or the button sits at (0,0) underneath the Roblox top bar buttons (menu and chat), and on phones under the notch or rounded corners. Fix it by setting ScreenGui.ScreenInsets = Enum.ScreenInsets.CoreUISafeInsets (this keeps content clear of the top bar and the device's safe area). Don't use ScreenInsets None or IgnoreGuiInset for interactive UI. Add a small offset or padding, for example a UIPadding. Use ScreenInsets.None only on a separate full-screen background ScreenGui. GuiService:GetGuiInset and the TopbarInset can help fine-tune.
Test both in Studio's Device Emulator on several phones and tablets.
T1:
```lua
-- ServerScriptService
local RS = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local BuyItem = RS.Remotes.BuyItem
local ITEMS = require(game.ServerStorage.ItemCatalog) -- [itemId] = {price=number, maxQty=number}

local lastCall = {}
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(p) lastCall[p] = nil end)

BuyItem.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, itemId, quantity)
    local now = os.clock()
    if lastCall[player] and now - lastCall[player] < 0.25 then return end
    lastCall[player] = now

    if typeof(itemId) ~= "string" or #itemId > 64 then return end
    if typeof(quantity) ~= "number" or quantity ~= quantity
        or quantity % 1 ~= 0 or quantity < 1 then return end

    local item = ITEMS[itemId]          -- server-side price, never trust client
    if not item or quantity > (item.maxQty or 99) then return end

    local data = PlayerData.get(player) -- server-owned data
    if not data then return end
    local cost = item.price * quantity
    if data.Coins < cost then return end

    data.Coins -= cost                  -- deduct before granting
    data.Inventory[itemId] = (data.Inventory[itemId] or 0) + quantity
    PlayerData.markDirty(player)
end)
```
The handler checks types, rejects NaN and fractions, uses a server-side catalog for prices, rate-limits calls, keeps the balance on the server and never takes a price or player argument from the client.
T2:
```lua
local LOCK_TTL = 30*60
local function load(player)
    local key = "u_"..player.UserId
    for attempt = 1, 5 do
        local ok, data = pcall(store.UpdateAsync, store, key, function(old)
            old = old or newProfile()
            local lock = old.Lock
            if lock and lock.JobId ~= game.JobId and os.time() - lock.Time < LOCK_TTL then
                return nil -- locked by another server: abort write
            end
            old.Lock = { JobId = game.JobId, Time = os.time() }
            return old
        end)
        if ok and data and data.Lock and data.Lock.JobId == game.JobId then
            return data
        end
        task.wait(attempt * 2) -- other server still releasing (teleport/rejoin)
    end
    player:Kick("Data busy, please rejoin")
end

local function save(player, data, release)
    pcall(store.UpdateAsync, store, key(player), function(old)
        if not old or not old.Lock or old.Lock.JobId ~= game.JobId then return nil end -- lost lock: don't overwrite
        data.Lock = release and nil or { JobId = game.JobId, Time = os.time() }
        return data
    end)
end
```
- Autosave every 60-120 seconds with save(p, d, false), which also refreshes the lock time.
- On PlayerRemoving, call save(p, d, true) to release the lock.
- In game:BindToClose, save and release for all players and wait for the saves to finish.
- Before teleporting, save and release, then teleport. The destination waits or retries until the lock is free.
- Never let gameplay modify data until the load succeeded.
- Process trades and receipts inside the same locked profile (with PurchaseId dedupe).
ProfileStore/ProfileService implement exactly this.

T4:
FireServer automatically sends the calling player as the first argument of OnServerEvent. Passing LocalPlayer yourself shifts everything along, so on the server `player` is the real sender, `amount` is the LocalPlayer Instance you passed, and 50 lands in a third parameter. `amount + 1` then does arithmetic on an Instance.
Fix: don't pass the player.
```lua
-- client
remote:FireServer(50)
-- server
remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, amount)
    if typeof(amount) ~= "number" or amount ~= amount then return end
    print(amount + 1)
end)
```
The same applies to RemoteFunction:InvokeServer. In the other direction, FireClient(player, ...) takes the player as a target, but OnClientEvent does not receive it.
Never trust a player argument sent by the client. Always use the implicit first parameter.
T5:
In Studio solo playtests the server and client start almost instantly. Your character and Player object can be created before your server Script finishes loading and connects PlayerAdded, for example if the script requires modules or yields first. The event for your player has already fired, so your handler never runs. Live servers start before anyone joins, which is why it works there.
The standard fix is to connect the handler and then also run it for players already in the game:
```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local function onPlayerAdded(player)
    local ls = Instance.new("Folder")
    ls.Name = "leaderstats"
    local coins = Instance.new("IntValue")
    coins.Name = "Coins"
    coins.Parent = ls
    ls.Parent = player
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded)
for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
    task.spawn(onPlayerAdded, p)
end
```
Also connect PlayerAdded before any yielding code (requires and WaitForChild calls), and make sure the folder is named exactly "leaderstats".

T8:
Several things are going on:
1. RenderFidelity can't be set by scripts at runtime. It's a Studio/plugin-level property that is baked when the mesh part is created or imported. Script assignments in a live game are ignored or error, so "changing it does nothing".
2. More importantly, Roblox's renderer now uses its own automatic mesh LOD and streaming. RenderFidelity is largely legacy: Precise is no longer a guarantee that full detail is kept at distance. The engine reduces distant meshes based on screen size, the client's graphics quality level and the device's memory, and on mobile and low-quality settings it always drops detail.
3. With StreamingEnabled, distant models can also be shown as low-detail model LOD imposters (Model.LevelOfDetail = Automatic/StreamingMesh) until they stream in.
What to do:
- Set the property in Studio, not in scripts, and accept that distant LOD is engine-controlled.
- For important hero models, set Model.LevelOfDetail = Disabled and ModelStreamingMode = Persistent (or Atomic) if they shouldn't be imposters.
- Keep a reasonable triangle count so the automatic LOD looks good.
- Test with graphics quality set to maximum to see the true behavior.
